documents.t: (EKS admin) This role grants Tabsdata the permissions it needs inside its own namespace. apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: <TABSDATA_ROLE> namespace: <TABSDATA_NAMESPACE> rules: - apiGroups: [ "" ] resources: [ "pods" ] verbs: [ "get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete", "deletecollection" ] - apiGroups: [ "" ] resources: [ "services", "configmaps", "secrets", "serviceaccounts" ] verbs: [ "get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete" ] - apiGroups: [ "" ] resources: [ "pods/log" ] verbs: [ "get", "list" ] - apiGroups: [ "" ] resources: [ "pods/portforward" ] verbs: [ "create" ] - apiGroups: [ "apps" ] resources: [ "deployments" ] verbs: [ "get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete", "deletecollection" ] - apiGroups: [ "policy" ] resources: [ "poddisruptionbudgets" ] verbs: [ "get", "list", "create", "update", "delete" ] - apiGroups: [ "networking.k8s.io" ] resources: [ "ingresses" ] verbs: [ "get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete" ] - apiGroups: [ "batch" ] resources: [ "jobs", "cronjobs" ] verbs: [ "get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete", "deletecollection" ] - apiGroups: [ "rbac.authorization.k8s.io" ] resources: [ "roles", "rolebindings" ] verbs: [ "get", "list", "create", "update", "delete" ] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: <TABSDATA_ROLE> namespace: <TABSDATA_NAMESPACE> subjects: - kind: Group name: <TABSDATA_GROUP> apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io roleRef: kind: Role name: <TABSDATA_ROLE> apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
documents.s: Create the namespace role and binding

documents.t: (EKS admin) A few of the checks Tabsdata runs cannot be expressed in a namespaced role, so they need a cluster role. All of them are read-only, and none grants any access beyond reading. Create the cluster role <TABSDATA_CLUSTER_ROLE> and bind it to the group <TABSDATA_GROUP>. apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: ClusterRole metadata: name: <TABSDATA_CLUSTER_ROLE> rules: - apiGroups: [ "" ] resources: [ "namespaces", "services", "nodes" ] verbs: [ "get", "list" ] - apiGroups: [ "karpenter.sh" ] resources: [ "nodepools" ] verbs: [ "get", "list" ] Finally, provide a <KUBECONFIG> file to the Tabsdata operator so the installation steps below can reach the cluster.
documents.s: Create the cluster role and binding

documents.t: (Tabsdata admin) Run these checks with the <KUBECONFIG> you were given, before going any further. kubectl auth can-i create deployments.apps kubectl auth can-i create cronjobs.batch kubectl auth can-i create secrets kubectl auth can-i create services kubectl auth can-i create roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io kubectl auth can-i create serviceaccounts kubectl auth can-i get pods/log kubectl auth can-i deletecollection pods kubectl auth can-i deletecollection deployments.apps kubectl auth can-i deletecollection jobs.batch kubectl auth can-i deletecollection cronjobs.batch kubectl auth can-i create pods/portforward kubectl auth can-i create ingresses.networking.k8s.io kubectl auth can-i create poddisruptionbudgets.policy kubectl auth can-i list namespaces kubectl auth can-i list services --all-namespaces kubectl auth can-i list nodes kubectl auth can-i list nodepools.karpenter.sh Every command must answer yes. If any command fails or answers no, check with your AWS EKS administrator before proceeding.

(RDS admin) Tabsdata stores its own state and the metadata for user data in PostgreSQL. Create an AWS RDS for PostgreSQL 18.4 instance with a database <TABSDATA_DATABASE>, using password authentication with <RDS_USERNAME> and <RDS_PASSWORD>. <RDS_USERNAME> must have the following permissions: Requirement Kind Statement CONNECT on <TABSDATA_DATABASE> privilege GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE <TABSDATA_DATABASE> TO <RDS_USERNAME>; CREATEROLE role attribute ALTER ROLE <RDS_USERNAME> CREATEROLE; CREATE on <TABSDATA_DATABASE> privilege GRANT CREATE ON DATABASE <TABSDATA_DATABASE> TO <RDS_USERNAME>; The RDS master username already satisfies all three, and owns any database it creates. The Tabsdata installation will create the necessary database schemas, roles and grants.

(RDS admin) One schema per Tabsdata component, inside <TABSDATA_DATABASE>: Schema Component <TABSDATA_DATABASE>_apiserver API server <TABSDATA_DATABASE>_aiagent AI agent Each schema holds that component's tables, indexes, views, triggers, row-level-security policies and baseline data. Three PostgreSQL roles. Roles are cluster-global, so their names must be unique across the whole RDS instance, which is why they derive from <TABSDATA_DATABASE>: Role Login Password Owns <TABSDATA_DATABASE>_apiserver LOGIN must be provided the API server schema <TABSDATA_DATABASE>_aiagent LOGIN must be provided the AI agent schema <TABSDATA_DATABASE>_app NOLOGIN none nothing The two login roles are the identities Tabsdata authenticates as, one per component. Their passwords are supplied during installation. <TABSDATA_DATABASE>_app is the role every Tabsdata connection then switches to, and the one row-level security is enforced against. It is shared by both components, owns nothing, and cannot be reached directly: it has no login and no password, and is used only internally by Tabsdata.
(S3 admin) Tabsdata uses AWS S3 bucket(s) for data storage. You need an S3 bucket <S3_BUCKET> in region <S3_REGION>, and full-access credentials for it: <S3_ACCESS_KEY> and <S3_SECRET_KEY>.

(EKS admin) note None of this applies to local access via kubectl port-forward, as described in Install Tabsdata on AWS EKS. Once installed, Tabsdata is running inside the cluster, but is not reachable from outside it. Public access is delivered by two AWS components layered on the cluster. In EKS, the apiserver Service is fronted by an alb-class Ingress, which the AWS Load Balancer Controller turns into an internet-facing Application Load Balancer targeting pod IPs, so the controller must already be installed with an IAM role permitting ELBv2 management, and the VPC's public subnets must carry the kubernetes.io/role/elb tag in every availability zone in use. That ALB listens on HTTP only, and its security group is locked to the AWS-managed CloudFront origin-facing prefix list (read from EC2), so it is not reachable directly. In front of it, a CloudFront distribution uses the ALB as a custom origin and serves viewers over HTTPS on its own *.cloudfront.net hostname, which is why no Route 53 record or ACM certificate is needed. Deployment of the distribution takes five to ten minutes; after that the instance answers only through CloudFront. Use the distribution's *.cloudfront.net URL as <TABSDATA_PUBLIC_URL>, and point your browser at it.
documents.s: Configure access from outside the cluster (over HTTPS)

documents.t: Before you begin AWS Services Setup for Tabsdata on EKS Tabsdata runs on Kubernetes as a set of long-running deployment pods, the API server, the AI agent and their supporting services, all installed into a single namespace. User functions are not part of those deployments: every publisher, subscriber and transformer execution is dispatched as its own Kubernetes job that starts, runs the function and exits, so function capacity scales with the cluster rather than with the instance. Neither the pods nor the jobs hold state. Table data lives in AWS S3 and all metadata lives in AWS RDS for PostgreSQL. Every step in this document is performed by the Tabsdata admin.

A Windows (x86), macOS (ARM64) or Linux (x86) client machine. Python 3.12.13 on the machine you install from. An AWS EKS Kubernetes cluster with x86 nodes. An AWS RDS for PostgreSQL instance running PostgreSQL 18.4, in the same region as the EKS cluster. An AWS S3 bucket, preferably in the same region as the EKS cluster. Network access: the EKS cluster must reach the RDS PostgreSQL instance, and the client machine must reach the EKS cluster.

You need to do these steps from a Windows, macOS or Linux machine that can access the EKS cluster. Create a clean Python virtual environment, point pip and uv at the Tabsdata index, then install Tabsdata in it. Keep these variables set for the rest of the install: the instance resolves the same Tabsdata version for itself when it is created. export PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL=https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ export UV_INDEX=https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ export UV_INDEX_STRATEGY=unsafe-best-match uv pip install "tabsdata[all]"==2.0.0 tabsdata-agent==2.0.0 With pip instead of uv: pip install "tabsdata[all]"==2.0.0 tabsdata-agent==2.0.0 Temporary Tabsdata 2.0.0 is not on PyPI yet, held up by an operational limit on uploads, so it installs from pypi.tabsdata.com instead. The version is required too: without it the resolver picks an older release from PyPI. tabsdata-agent ships as its own package and the AI features need it. Drop the variables and the pins once the packages reach PyPI. If you do not have an EKS cluster and namespace ready, or you do not yet have a <KUBECONFIG> that reaches them, AWS Services Setup for Tabsdata on EKS explains how they must be configured. note The MySQL and PostgreSQL CDC connectors need database drivers that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. If you use either one, see Installing Third-Party Database Drivers before you continue, since the requirements file is read during the setup below.

Collect these values before you start. The install asks for all of them, and none of them can be filled in later without editing the instance. Value Description AWS RDS for PostgreSQL <RDS_HOST> Hostname of the RDS instance <RDS_PORT> Port of the RDS instance <TABSDATA_DATABASE> Database Tabsdata installs into <RDS_USERNAME> User Tabsdata connects as during setup <RDS_PASSWORD> Password for that user AWS S3 <S3_BUCKET> Bucket used for data storage <S3_REGION> Region of the bucket <S3_ACCESS_KEY> Access key with full access to the bucket <S3_SECRET_KEY> Secret key for that access key AWS EKS <TABSDATA_CLUSTER> Cluster Tabsdata is installed into <TABSDATA_NAMESPACE> Empty namespace reserved for this instance <KUBECONFIG> Path to a kubeconfig file that reaches the cluster LLM provider <OPENAI_API_KEY> / <ANTHROPIC_API_KEY> LLM API key, if the AI integration is enabled Chosen during the install Value Description <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> Name of the Tabsdata instance <TABSDATA_APISERVER_PASSWORD> Password you pick for the API server database role <TABSDATA_AIAGENT_PASSWORD> Password you pick for the AI agent database role

tdkserver init --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> --provider eks --kubeconfig <KUBECONFIG> --namespace <TABSDATA_NAMESPACE> This will create a folder ~/.tabsdata/instances/<TABSDATA_INSTANCE>/ with files that must be configured (details follow) to complete the Tabsdata installation. The Tabsdata configuration files to edit are in the ~/.tabsdata/instances/<TABSDATA_INSTANCE>/init/input/configs/ folder.

The database configuration is split across two files, dbmanager.database.yaml and apiserver.database.yaml. The first one is used during setup only. The second one is used for regular operations. The database credentials are extracted and stored encrypted in the EKS Kubernetes secret store. The RDS information must be set in the dbmanager.database.yaml file. Configuration file dbmanager.database.yaml: database_server: postgres: host: <RDS_HOST> port: <RDS_PORT> database: <TABSDATA_DATABASE> username: <RDS_USERNAME> password: <RDS_PASSWORD> ssl_mode: ${{system:tdk_database_ssl_mode}} ssl_root_cert: ${{system:tdk_database_ssl_root_cert}} pool: min_connections: 1 max_connections: 2 acquire_timeout: 30 max_lifetime: 1800 idle_timeout: 30 test_before_acquire: true The apiserver.database.yaml file requires two passwords, which you must provide. The Tabsdata installation creates the <TABSDATA_DATABASE>_apiserver and <TABSDATA_DATABASE>_aiagent roles and sets these passwords on them. Configuration file apiserver.database.yaml: database: apiserver: postgres: password: <TABSDATA_APISERVER_PASSWORD> pool: min_connections: 5 max_connections: 50 acquire_timeout: 30 max_lifetime: 3600 idle_timeout: 60 test_before_acquire: true aiagent: postgres: password: <TABSDATA_AIAGENT_PASSWORD> pool: min_connections: 1 max_connections: 10 acquire_timeout: 30 max_lifetime: 3600 idle_timeout: 60 test_before_acquire: true

Tabsdata on EKS uses AWS S3 as its storage layer. It is recommended that the S3 bucket(s) be in the same region as the EKS cluster. Three mounts must be configured: ROOT, BUNDLES and IMAGES. They can all use the same bucket, as long as the paths differ. Each entry must be configured with its corresponding region, access key and secret key. The credentials are extracted and stored encrypted in the EKS Kubernetes secret store. Configuration file apiserver.storage.yaml: warning The S3 URI must end with /. storage: mounts: - id: ROOT path: / uri: s3://<S3_BUCKET>/root/ options: aws_region: <S3_REGION> aws_access_key_id: <S3_ACCESS_KEY> aws_secret_access_key: <S3_SECRET_KEY> - id: BUNDLES path: /bundles uri: s3://<S3_BUCKET>/bundles/ options: aws_region: <S3_REGION> aws_access_key_id: <S3_ACCESS_KEY> aws_secret_access_key: <S3_SECRET_KEY> - id: IMAGES path: /images uri: s3://<S3_BUCKET>/images/ options: aws_region: <S3_REGION> aws_access_key_id: <S3_ACCESS_KEY> aws_secret_access_key: <S3_SECRET_KEY>

To enable the Tabsdata AI integration, an LLM API key must be provided. Tabsdata currently supports Anthropic and OpenAI. The API keys are extracted and stored encrypted in the EKS Kubernetes secret store. Configuration file aiagent.yaml: port: ${{system:tdk_aiagent_public_port}} allow_writes: true ai_providers: openai: api_key: <OPENAI_API_KEY> model: openai/gpt-5.4 anthropic: api_key: <ANTHROPIC_API_KEY> model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6 hybrid_search: embedder: fastembed embedding_model: BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 device: cpu cache_dir: null offline: false

Every pod resolves Python packages of its own, so the pods need the Tabsdata index as well as the machine you install from. Configuration file tabsdata.yaml: pods: global: # Every entry here is injected as an environment variable into every # container of every pod. A variable a container declares itself is left # alone, so these are defaults rather than overrides. envs: UV_INDEX: https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ UV_DEFAULT_INDEX: https://pypi.org/simple/ UV_INDEX_STRATEGY: unsafe-best-match warning Tabsdata 2.0.0 is not on PyPI yet due to an operational upload limit. UV_DEFAULT_INDEX keeps PyPI as the default source for other dependencies, while unsafe-best-match allows uv to resolve packages across both PyPI and the Tabsdata index. Remove this section once Tabsdata 2.0.0 is available on PyPI.
Check that nothing is still missing before creating the instance. tdkserver check-cfg --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE>
tdkserver create --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> Verify the Tabsdata instance state. tdkserver inspect --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE>
tdkserver start --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> tdkserver status --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE>

Use port forwarding to verify Tabsdata is running. kubectl port-forward --kubeconfig <KUBECONFIG> --namespace <TABSDATA_NAMESPACE> service/net-apiserver 2457:2457 Leave that command running, and use http://127.0.0.1:2457 as <TABSDATA_URL> in the next step. Port 2457 is the default API server port; if the instance was given a different base port, use that one instead. Port forwarding is meant for verifying the installation. Expose Tabsdata properly before using it.
tdk login --server <TABSDATA_URL> --user admin --password tabsdata tdk status
documents.s: Log in to the Tabsdata instance

documents.t: The configuration is now stored in the instance, so you can delete the local setup files. They contain the passwords and access keys you entered. rm -rf ~/.tabsdata/instances/<TABSDATA_INSTANCE>/init

The instance is now running, but only reachable through the port forward above. To reach the API server on an address outside the cluster, AWS Services Setup for Tabsdata on EKS explains how it must be exposed over HTTPS.
Run your first data integration: Run Your First Data Integration.

All sizing lives in the instance's configs/tabsdata.yaml. Pod descriptors carry none of their own, so what is written there is what the cluster receives. service covers the pods that run alongside the instance; its own resources apply to every service pod, and the named entries (apiserver, aiagent, aiembeddings, aimetadata) override them for one component each, so a pod with no entry of its own, a manager, inspector or loader, uses the service values directly. function covers the pods created per execution and applies to all of them uniformly. Service requests are a fixed per-instance cost: sum them and multiply by the number of instances the cluster will hold. Function requests are a per-concurrent-run cost. Disk is usually the binding constraint on both sides, since aiagent alone asks for 64Gi, as does every function run, which is why both node pools select instance types with local NVMe. pods: service: priority: tabsdata-service resources: # dbmanager / pymanager / inspector / venvloader cpu: "2" memory: 1Gi disk: 16Gi placement: selectors: {} tolerations: [] aiagent: # overrides the above, for this component only resources: cpu: "2" memory: 8Gi disk: 64Gi function: priority: tabsdata-function resources: cpu: "1" memory: 16Gi disk: 64Gi placement: selectors: {} tolerations: - key: workload # must match the functions pool taint value: batch effect: NoSchedule Values are examples. Set them from the actual footprint of the components in use, then confirm each pool's node class can still satisfy the largest single pod. Retrieve and upload the file with tdkserver get-cfg / tdkserver put-cfg.
documents.s: Sizing the service and function pods

documents.t: Before you begin Install Tabsdata tdkserver init produces an editable config folder for a Tabsdata instance within ~/.tabsdata, pre-filled with default values. Initialize an instance​ tdkserver init --instance myinstance --provider kminus The config folder is written to ~/.tabsdata/instances/myinstance/. The default configuration is what is used by tdkserver quickstart which bundles initializing, creating, and starting a server

tdkserver init --instance myinstance --provider kminus The config folder is written to ~/.tabsdata/instances/myinstance/. The default configuration is what is used by tdkserver quickstart which bundles initializing, creating, and starting a server

Edit the config files the command produced, if you need to change anything. Create a Server using the config Start a Server. To accept the defaults and get all three in one command, use Quickstart a Server instead. Deploying on AWS EKS starts here too, with values for the database, storage and cluster. See Install Tabsdata on AWS EKS.

Tabsdata requires the tabsdata python package, which is installable through pip and requires no admin or root privileges. Requirements Machine with a supported OS Linux (x86) macOS (Apple Silicon/ARM64) Windows (x86) Python 3.12

Using a virtual environment provides a layer of isolation and prevents interference from other python environments on your machine. macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) conda uv pyenv venv conda create -n tabsdata python=3.12 -y conda activate tabsdata uv venv --python 3.12 .venv source .venv/bin/activate pyenv install 3.12 pyenv local 3.12 python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate conda uv pyenv venv conda create -n tabsdata python=3.12 -y conda activate tabsdata uv venv --python 3.12 .venv .venv\Scripts\activate pyenv install 3.12 pyenv local 3.12 python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate

warning Tabsdata 2.0.0 is temporarily hosted on the Tabsdata package index rather than PyPI. Until 2.0.0 is available on PyPI, configure pip and uv to use the Tabsdata index and explicitly install version 2.0.0. export PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL=https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ export UV_INDEX=https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ export UV_INDEX_STRATEGY=unsafe-best-match Keep these environment variables set until the Tabsdata Instance has been created and run successfully. tdkserver quickstart creates a separate Python environment for the instance and also needs access to the Tabsdata index.

warning Until 2.0.0 is fully hosted on pypi, please make sure to specify ==2.0.0 as the version for installation. Future releases will not have this requirement uv pip uv pip install "tabsdata[all]"==2.0.0 pip install "tabsdata[all]"==2.0.0 Where the server runs Tabsdata runs on a Kubernetes cluster, and this install uses kminus: a lightweight Kubernetes that runs pods as native processes in your Python environment instead of Docker containers, so it needs no root or admin access. To run on AWS EKS instead, start with AWS Services Setup, then Install on EKS.

Before you begin Install Tabsdata tdkserver quickstart bundles initializing, creating, and starting a Tabsdata server into a single command, using a default configuration for compute and storage. Set the Tabsdata index​ Temporary quickstart builds the instance its own Python environment and installs the same Tabsdata version into it, so it needs the Tabsdata index in its environment. Export these in the same terminal before running it, and keep them set through instance creation and the instance's first run: macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) export UV_INDEX=https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ export UV_INDEX_STRATEGY=unsafe-best-match $env:UV_INDEX = "https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/" $env:UV_INDEX_STRATEGY = "unsafe-best-match" Dropping them before the instance has created and run once leaves the server unable to resolve Tabsdata. Tabsdata 2.0.0 is not on PyPI yet, held up by an operational limit on uploads, so this is required until the packages reach PyPI. Start a Tabsdata server​ tdkserver quickstart runs in the foreground and keeps running. That's normal. Leave it open and use a new terminal for the following steps. tdkserver quickstart --instance myinstance note If you plan to use the MySQL or PostgreSQL CDC connectors, they need database drivers that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. Pass a requirements file with --reqs-td, as described in Installing Third-Party Database Drivers. Adding them later means re-running the installation. Check Tabsdata Server Status​ In your new terminal: tdkserver status Log in​ tdk login --server localhost --user admin --password tabsdata

Temporary quickstart builds the instance its own Python environment and installs the same Tabsdata version into it, so it needs the Tabsdata index in its environment. Export these in the same terminal before running it, and keep them set through instance creation and the instance's first run: macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) export UV_INDEX=https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ export UV_INDEX_STRATEGY=unsafe-best-match $env:UV_INDEX = "https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/" $env:UV_INDEX_STRATEGY = "unsafe-best-match" Dropping them before the instance has created and run once leaves the server unable to resolve Tabsdata. Tabsdata 2.0.0 is not on PyPI yet, held up by an operational limit on uploads, so this is required until the packages reach PyPI.

tdkserver quickstart runs in the foreground and keeps running. That's normal. Leave it open and use a new terminal for the following steps. tdkserver quickstart --instance myinstance note If you plan to use the MySQL or PostgreSQL CDC connectors, they need database drivers that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. Pass a requirements file with --reqs-td, as described in Installing Third-Party Database Drivers. Adding them later means re-running the installation.
In your new terminal: tdkserver status
tdk login --server localhost --user admin --password tabsdata
quickstart bundles initializing, creating, and running a server using a default configuration. For custom deployment, do Initialize a Server, Create a Server, and Start a Server.

Before you begin Create a Server tdkserver start brings up the services of an instance that tdkserver create already built. Until the instance is running, tdk has nothing to connect to. Step 1Start the instance tdkserver start --instance myinstance The command prints the values it resolved and waits for confirmation. Pass --yes to skip the prompt, and --verbose to watch each step as it runs rather than a progress line. Step 2Confirm the server is up tdkserver status --instance myinstance Step 3Log in tdk login --server localhost:2457 --user admin Use the base port the instance was created with. login prompts for the password rather than taking it as an argument, which keeps it out of your shell history. From here, tdk project create and the rest of the CLI reach the running server.

--loglevel sets how much the kminus orchestrator and pod runner record, from trace through error: tdkserver start --instance myinstance --loglevel debug The value is saved as the instance's log level and reused by later starts, so a plain tdkserver start keeps whatever was set last. The flag applies only to the kminus provider.
tdkserver restart stops and starts in one command, which is what picks up a configuration change on a running instance.
The server is ready for work. Create a project to hold your groups and collections. See tdkserver start for the full option list.

Before you begin Start a Server tdkserver stop shuts down a running instance's services and leaves everything else in place. The instance stays registered, its configuration is untouched, and the tables and function code it holds survive, so a later start picks up where the stop left off. Step 1Stop the instance tdkserver stop --instance myinstance The command prints the values it resolved and waits for confirmation. Pass --yes to skip the prompt. Step 2Confirm it stopped tdkserver status --instance myinstance

Stopping the server stops its workers with it, so a function run in flight does not finish. Nothing partial is committed: a run only commits when every function in its execution plan succeeds, so an interrupted run leaves the tables at the version they held beforehand. Check for active work before stopping: tdk fnrun list --status running
A configuration edit reaches a running instance through a restart rather than a stop: tdkserver restart --instance myinstance
Start a Server to bring the same instance back up, or Delete a Server to discard it. See tdkserver stop for the full option list.

Some Tabsdata connectors depend on Python database drivers that Tabsdata cannot redistribute because of their licensing terms. These drivers are not included in the Tabsdata distribution, and are not installed by default. If you use one of the affected connectors, you must install its driver explicitly as part of the Tabsdata installation. Doing so is a deliberate, one-time step: you choose the driver versions, and you accept the licence terms of the driver's publisher.

Install only the drivers for the connectors you actually use. Connector Required package MySQL, MySQL CDC, MariaDB mysql-connector-python PostgreSQL, PostgreSQL CDC psycopg2-binary If you are not using any of these connectors, no action is required.

In both installation flows you supply a plain pip requirements file listing the drivers and their versions. Pin exact versions (==) so that installations are reproducible and so that an upgrade is always an explicit decision: mysql-connector-python==9.6.0 psycopg2-binary==2.9.11 Remove any line for a connector you do not use.

Create the requirements file anywhere on the machine you are installing from. The quick start flow reads whatever path you give it, so the name is yours to choose; this page uses requirements-td.txt, the name the EKS flow requires. Pass it to quickstart with --reqs-td: tdkserver quickstart --reqs-td ./requirements-td.txt The drivers are installed into the instance's Python environment as part of the quick start.

For an EKS installation the requirements file lives inside the instance's init assets, under a fixed name. Initialise the instance: tdkserver init Edit the requirements file in the instance config directory. init always creates it, so the file is already there: ~/.tabsdata/instances/<TABSDATA_INSTANCE>/init/assets/configs/requirements-td.txt Replace <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> with your instance name. Add one driver specification per line, as shown in Declaring the drivers. Continue with the rest of the Tabsdata EKS setup instructions. The drivers are baked into the function runner environment during setup, so they are available to connector functions at execution time. note Unlike the quick start flow, there is no command-line option here and the location is fixed. Tabsdata always reads requirements-td.txt from the instance configs directory; a file under any other name, or in any other directory, is ignored.

The requirements file is only read at installation time, so adding a driver means re-running the installation. The instance's configs/ directory from the original installation must still be intact. That is where the requirements file lives and where the installation reads its configuration from. Add the driver to requirements-td.txt in the instance configs directory. Delete the installation: tdkserver delete Re-create it: tdkserver create Until the driver is present in the environment that executes functions, any connector that needs it will fail at run time. note tdkserver delete does not erase user data or metadata. It tears down the installation, not its contents. note A future version of Tabsdata will provide a dedicated command for updating function virtual environment requirements, making the delete/create cycle unnecessary.
documents.s: Adding a driver to an existing installation

documents.t: A connector fails with a missing-module error. The driver for that connector is not installed in the environment running the function. Confirm that the package is listed in the requirements file, that the file was picked up by the installation flow (correct --reqs-td path, or correct filename and directory for EKS), and that the setup step has been re-run since the file changed. The driver fails to build during installation. Prefer the binary distributions named above (psycopg2-binary rather than psycopg2). If a build is still attempted, the installation environment is missing the compiler or client-library headers that the driver's source distribution needs.

Each page here covers one task, in the order you'd hit them: a server has to exist before you can register a publisher, and a table has to exist before anything can transform it. For worked end-to-end projects against real systems, see Advanced Tutorials.

Before you begin Create a Project A collection holds functions and the tables they write. The group it is created in decides which kind of function it can hold, and that is fixed for the collection's life. A source or destination collection also carries exactly one connection, and it is created together with that connection rather than separately. Step 1Create a data product collection, for transformers tdk collection create \ --proj finance \ --name reporting \ --group default \ --description "Reporting tables" A collection in default, or in any group you created, holds transformers and takes no connection. Passing --conn-file here is an error. Step 2Or create a source collection, with its connection tdk collection create \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-postgres.yaml --conn-file is required for sources and destinations. The CLI derives the group from the connection's direction, so --group acts as an assertion: a mismatch is an error rather than a preference. Step 3Confirm it exists tdk collection list --proj finance tdk collection get --proj finance --name sales_src tdk collection get prints a data product collection's type as Data Factory, which is the same thing the docs call a data product.

--storage-path is the logical prefix for the collection's artifacts, written as base_path in the API. Unset, it inherits the project's prefix, and the resolved value is readable as effective_base_path. Changing it later is not retroactive: existing data versions keep the path they were written under, and only new artifacts use the new prefix.

Register a function into the collection. A source collection takes publishers, a destination collection takes subscribers, and a data product collection takes transformers. See tdk collection create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection Deleting a collection deletes its functions and tables, and freezes functions elsewhere that read from it. It takes a typed confirmation. Step 1Check what depends on the collection tdk table list --proj finance --coll sales_src Functions in other collections that read these tables are frozen by the delete, so it is worth knowing which tables those are. Step 2Delete it tdk collection delete \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src --confirm takes the literal string delete.

The delete is a soft delete with a cascade, in this order: The collection row is renamed to deleted_<id>, which frees the original name for immediate reuse. Functions in other collections that depend on its tables are set to Frozen. A frozen function stays registered and stops running until it is re-registered against tables that exist. Its tables, triggers and dependencies are set to Deleted, and its own functions are set to Deleted. Scheduled cron and stage workers are stopped. After the commit, the connection's stored content is deleted on a best-effort basis. Function status is one of Active, Frozen or Deleted, so a frozen function is visible in a listing rather than silently gone. See tdk collection delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection tdk collection update changes a collection's name, its description, its storage path, or the connection it carries. What it cannot change is the collection's type or the group it belongs to: both are fixed at creation. Step 1Rename it, or change its description tdk collection update \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --new-name sales_source \ --description "Postgres sales tables" Renaming a source or destination collection renames its connection too, since the connection is named by the collection. Step 2Or replace the connection tdk collection update \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --conn-file conn-postgres-prod.yaml The connector kind is fixed for the collection's life, so the replacement document has to be the same kind. Pointing a publisher at a different database means a new connection of the same kind, not a different connector. Step 3Check the result tdk collection get --proj finance --name sales_source A request that changes nothing is rejected: The collection update request has nothing to update. When a rename and a connection change are passed together, the rename is applied first.

The collection's type, and therefore its group, are immutable. There is no command that moves a collection to another group, and CollectionUpdate carries no field for it. Changing connectors means deleting the collection and creating it again. --storage-path applies to new artifacts only. Existing data versions keep the path stamped at write time. See tdk collection update for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project A group sits inside a project and holds collections. Which group a collection is created in fixes what that collection can hold, and that choice is permanent. Three groups exist in every project already: sources for publishers, destinations for subscribers, and default for transformers. A group you create yourself holds transformers too, so the reason to add one is organising a pipeline rather than unlocking anything new. Step 1Create the group tdk group create \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --description "Raw ingested data" --proj names the project the group belongs to, and can be omitted when a project is pinned. Collections created in bronze hold transformers, the same as default. Step 2Confirm it exists tdk group list --proj finance The three seeded groups are listed alongside it. System groups cannot be renamed or deleted.

Collections in a user-created group hold transformers, which default already does, so grouping is organisational. The medallion layout, bronze then silver then gold, is a common convention for naming the stages of a pipeline; it is a docs convention rather than something Tabsdata enforces.
documents.s: Why add a group at all

documents.t: Create a Collection in the group. See tdk group create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Group Deleting a group deletes the collections inside it. Like the other deletes, it takes a typed confirmation. Step 1Check what the group holds tdk collection list --proj finance --group bronze Every collection listed here goes with the group. Step 2Delete it tdk group delete \ --proj finance \ --name bronze --confirm takes the literal string delete. The three system groups cannot be deleted, so this only ever applies to a group you created.

The group's collections are deleted with it, along with their tables and functions. Functions in other collections that depended on those tables are frozen rather than deleted: they stay registered and stop running until they are re-registered against tables that exist. See tdk group delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Group tdk group update changes a group's name or description. The collections inside it are untouched, and so is what those collections are allowed to hold. Step 1Rename the group, or change its description tdk group update \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --new-name raw \ --description "Raw ingested data" --name is the current name and --new-name the replacement. Either --new-name or --description is enough on its own. Step 2Check the result tdk group get --proj finance --name raw The three system groups, default, sources and destinations, cannot be updated at all.

A collection's type follows from the group it was created in, and renaming the group does not revisit that. A collection created in sources still holds publishers after the group is called something else. See tdk group update for the full option list.
documents.s: What a rename does not change

documents.t: Before you begin Install Tabsdata Start a Server A project is the outermost resource within Tabsdata server and allows full isolation from workflows and resources in other projects. Step 1Create the project tdk project create \ --name finance \ --description "Subscription billing" --name starts with a letter and continues with letters, digits or underscores, up to 100 characters, and has to be unique on the server. --description is optional and capped at 200 characters. Step 2Confirm it exists and see its groups tdk project list tdk group list --proj finance The three seeded groups appear straight away. A collection created in sources holds publishers, one in destinations holds subscribers, and one in default or any group you add yourself holds transformers.

Most commands take --proj to say which project they act on. Pinning one makes it the default: tdk project pin --name finance Every later command then acts on finance unless it passes --proj explicitly.
documents.s: Pin it, so later commands need no --proj

documents.t: A project on its own holds nothing. Create a collection in one of its groups: Create a Collection. See tdk project create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project warning Deleting a project deletes all resources nested inside of it, including function code, execution logs, and table data. This action cannot be reversed. Step 1Check what the project holds tdk group list --proj finance tdk collection list --proj finance Step 2Delete it tdk project delete \ --name finance --confirm takes the literal string delete. Anything else, including y or yes, cancels the command and leaves the project standing.

Every group and collection in the project is deleted with it, along with the tables those collections held and the functions registered in them. The project's name is freed and can be reused immediately. See tdk project delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project tdk project update changes a project's name or its description. Both are metadata: renaming a project does not move, rebuild or re-path anything inside it. Step 1Rename the project, or change its description tdk project update \ --name finance \ --new-name billing \ --description "Subscription billing and dunning" --name names the project as it stands now; --new-name is what it becomes. Passing only --description changes the description and leaves the name alone. Step 2Check the result tdk project get --name billing A request that changes nothing is rejected rather than silently accepted, with The project update request has nothing to update.

The project keeps its id, its groups, its collections and their data. Anything referring to the project by id keeps working; anything referring to it by name, a pinned project or a script passing --proj, needs the new name. See tdk project update for the full option list.
documents.s: What a rename does not change

documents.t: This is the pipeline you build in the Getting Started tutorial. Click any node to inspect its Python code or table schema. Tabsdata · Tutorial Pipeline · Execution View Publisher pub pub Publisher Committed Table persons persons //tutorial ✓Data Available Transformer tfr tfr Transformer Committed Table spanish spanish //tutorial ✓Data Available Table french french //tutorial ✓Data Available Table german german //tutorial ✓Data Available Click any node to inspect code or schema

The pipeline has three stages: Publisher (pub) — reads CSV files from disk, renames columns, and writes to the persons table. Transformer (tfr) — reads persons, filters rows by language, and writes three output tables. Tables — spanish, french, and german each hold the filtered rows for subscribers to consume. The dashed blue line between persons → tfr represents a data-dependency edge: the transformer triggers automatically whenever persons is updated.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project This tutorial shows how to set up an Amazon S3 publisher that reads one or more files out of an S3 bucket and writes them into one or more Tabsdata Tables

A Connection is a resource that stores the configuration and credentials needed to access an external system. Publishers use the credentials stored in a connection to authenticate with AWS. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type s3-file-in --file conn-s3.yaml This creates a connection template document within your working directory under the file name specified in the --file cli command. Step 2Fill in the bucket, the region, and the credentials within the connection document tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn spec: bucket: 'acme-ingest' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional Fill in the bucket name, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key, and base path. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-s3.yaml

The connection file in the previous step is passed into Tabsdata by binding it to a Collection. A source collection is created together with its connection, so a new collection and an existing one take different commands. Step 4Bind connection to a new or existing collection Create a New Collection Attach to an Existing Collection tdk collection create --name hr_files --group sources --conn-file conn-s3.yaml tdk collection update --name hr_files --conn-file conn-s3.yaml Every publisher registered in hr_files reads through this one connection, and the collection accepts as many publishers as you want to put in it. To point the same publisher code at a different bucket, register it into a second source collection whose connection names that bucket. The code stays untouched.

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_files.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src @publisher( source=S3Src( paths=["departments.csv", "employees.csv"], ), output_tables=["departments", "employees"], ) def read_files( departments: TableFramesSpec, employees: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (departments[0], employees[0]) Each entry in paths fills one function argument with a list of frames (TableFramesSpec), one frame per matched file. An exact key matches one file, so its slot is a single-element list, which is why the example returns departments[0]. The function returns one frame per name in output_tables, in the same order. Paths resolve relative to the connection's base_path, so the publisher names objects and never the bucket. Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll hr_files --path read_files.py::read_files Re-register after every code change. See Publishers for the rest of the registration flags.

Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll hr_files --name read_files Tabsdata imports the matching files on the server and writes one versioned table per path. Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll hr_files tdk table data --coll hr_files --name departments
documents.s: Trigger it and read the tables

documents.t: function.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src @publisher( source=S3Src( paths=[ "landing/invoices.parquet", ], ), output_tables=["invoices"], ) def read_invoices(invoices: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if invoices is None: return (None,) return (invoices[0],) paths:list[str]required format:SrcFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional initial_last_modified:datetime | Noneoptional file_info:FileInfo | Noneoptional src_cfg:dict[str, Any]optional trigger_by:list[str] | CronTriggeroptional on_tables:list[DataQuality]optional

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when you call tdk fn trigger. Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when the publisher should poll the bucket on a fixed UTC schedule. The cron mask is standard 5-field crontab syntax, with optional start and end bounds for a limited run window. This fits when producers drop files into S3 on their own rhythm and Tabsdata should check hourly, nightly, or on another predictable cadence. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src @publisher( source=S3Src( paths=["landing/invoices.parquet"], ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices[0],)

Set initial_last_modified to ingest only new files instead of re-reading everything on every run. The first run imports files modified at or after the timestamp, and the cutoff advances on its own afterwards, so each trigger imports only what arrived since the previous one. A path that matches no new files fills its slot with None rather than an empty list. Returning None for a table tells Tabsdata to keep the previous version as current instead of committing a new one: read_when_available.py @publisher( source=S3Src(paths=["landing/invoices.parquet"]), output_tables=["invoices"], ) def read_when_available(invoices: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if invoices is None: return (None,) return (invoices[0],)

Access denied or authentication errors. Secrets are read out of the connection file when the collection is created, so an edit made after that point has not reached the server. Re-run tdk connection validate --file conn-s3.yaml to check the document, then tdk collection update --conn-file conn-s3.yaml to send the corrected credentials. Check too that the key pair has read access to the bucket and the prefix. No files imported. Paths are relative to the connection's base_path, so check the path against it. With initial_last_modified set, files older than the current cutoff are skipped by design. Wrong columns or parse errors. The format comes from the file extension. Force it with format and tune parsing with format_cfg. A run succeeds but a table has no new version. Its path matched no new files and the function returned None for that slot, which means keep the current version.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Azure Blob Storage connector lets a publisher read data out of Azure Blob Storage and land it in Tabsdata as versioned tables. Each entry in paths is an exact key or a glob pattern, and each entry fills one input slot and produces one output table.
documents.s: Publish data from Azure Blob Storage

documents.t: The connection holds the container, the credentials, and the optional base_path, so the publisher names blobs and never the container. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type az-file-in --file conn-azure.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the container and the credentials tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.azureblob:AzureBlobSrcConn spec: container: 'acme-ingest' credentials: kind: azureAccountKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AzureAccountKey spec: account_name: 'secret:mystorageaccount' account_key: 'secret:8Zs0RExAmPlEkEy0000==' container:strrequired credentials:AzureAccountKeyrequired base_path:stroptional Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-azure.yaml

A source collection is created together with its connection, which is why there is no separate collection step ahead of this one and why --conn-file is required rather than optional. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name hr_files --group sources --conn-file conn-azure.yaml create validates the document once more, strips the secret values out client-side, and sends both parts to the server. Every publisher registered in hr_files from now on reads through this one connection, and the collection accepts as many publishers as you want to put in it.

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_files.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.azureblob import AzureBlobSrc @publisher( source=AzureBlobSrc( paths=["departments.csv", "employees_*.csv"], file_info="uri", ), output_tables=["departments", "employees"], ) def read_files( departments: TableFrameSpec, employees: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (departments, employees[0]) Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll hr_files --path read_files.py::read_files Re-register after every code change. See Publishers for the rest of the registration flags.

Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll hr_files --name read_files Tabsdata imports the matching files on the server and writes one versioned table per path. Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll hr_files tdk table data --coll hr_files --name departments
documents.s: Trigger it and read the tables

documents.t: Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when you call tdk fn trigger. Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: Azure Blob publishers can be driven by a schedule or by another Tabsdata table. Pick the mode that matches how files arrive in the container. 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when the container should be scanned on a fixed cadence for newly uploaded blobs. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.azureblob import AzureBlobSrc @publisher( source=AzureBlobSrc( paths=["landing/invoices_*.parquet"], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices[0],)

Use relative blob paths in AzureBlobSrc(paths=[...]). Format selection, wildcard expansion, initial_last_modified, and file_info behave the same way as the S3 file connector. In practice: Use a stable base_path for the collection and keep publisher paths relative under it. Use wildcard patterns when upstream processes upload many partitioned files. Prefer file_info="uri" when the blob path should survive into downstream processing.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Databricks connector lets a publisher read data out of Databricks and land it in Tabsdata as versioned tables. Each entry in queries produces one output table. A query can carry {placeholder} names that initial_values fills in, so one publisher reads the same tables out of a different catalog or schema without the SQL changing.

The connection holds the workspace URL, the token, the staging volume, and the warehouse the read goes through. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type databricks-bulk-in --file conn-databricks.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the workspace URL, token, volume, and warehouse tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.databricks:DatabricksSrcConn spec: host_url: 'secret:https://dbc-00000000.cloud.databricks.com' token: 'secret:dapi0example0token0000' volume: 'main.default.tabsdata_stage' host_url:Secretrequired token:Secretrequired volume:strrequired warehouse:stroptional warehouse_id:stroptional catalog:stroptional schema:stroptional Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-databricks.yaml

A source collection is created together with its connection, which is why there is no separate collection step ahead of this one and why --conn-file is required rather than optional. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name world --group sources --conn-file conn-databricks.yaml create validates the document once more, strips the secret values out client-side, and sends both parts to the server. Every publisher registered in world from now on reads through this one connection, and the collection accepts as many publishers as you want to put in it.

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_world.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksSrc @publisher( source=DatabricksSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM {catalog}.{schema}.country", "SELECT * FROM {catalog}.{schema}.city", ], initial_values={"catalog": "main", "schema": "default"}, ), output_tables=["country", "city"], ) def read_world( country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (country, city) Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll world --path read_world.py::read_world Re-register after every code change. See Publishers for the rest of the registration flags.

Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll world --name read_world Tabsdata runs the queries on the server and writes one versioned table per query. Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll world tdk table data --coll world --name city
documents.s: Trigger it and read the tables

documents.t: Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when you call tdk fn trigger. Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: Databricks publishers can run on a schedule or from changes in another Tabsdata table. 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when Databricks should be polled on a fixed cadence. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksSrc @publisher( source=DatabricksSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM {catalog}.{schema}.invoices"], initial_values={"catalog": "main", "schema": "default"}, ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices,)

Databricks query interpolation uses Python str.format-style substitution, not SQLAlchemy bind parameters. In practice that means your query contains placeholders like {catalog} or {as_of_date}, seeded by initial_values and updated between runs if needed. Databricks publishers can run on a schedule or from changes in another Tabsdata table. 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when Databricks should be polled on a fixed cadence. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksSrc @publisher( source=DatabricksSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM {catalog}.{schema}.invoices"], initial_values={"catalog": "main", "schema": "default"}, ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices,)

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Db2 connector lets a publisher read data out of Db2 and land it in Tabsdata as versioned tables. Each entry in queries produces one output table, so the query list and the table list line up position by position.

The connection holds the URI and the credentials, so the publisher holds SQL and nothing about where the database is. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type db2-sql-in --file conn-db2.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the URI and the credentials tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.db2:Db2SrcConn spec: uri: 'db2+ibm_db://db.internal:50000/world' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_reader' password: 'secret:example-password' uri:strrequired credentials:UserPasswordrequired Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-db2.yaml

A source collection is created together with its connection, which is why there is no separate collection step ahead of this one and why --conn-file is required rather than optional. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name world --group sources --conn-file conn-db2.yaml create validates the document once more, strips the secret values out client-side, and sends both parts to the server. Every publisher registered in world from now on reads through this one connection, and the collection accepts as many publishers as you want to put in it.

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_world.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2Src @publisher( source=Db2Src( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM COUNTRY", "SELECT * FROM CITY", ], ), output_tables=["country", "city"], ) def read_world( country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (country, city) Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll world --path read_world.py::read_world Re-register after every code change. See Publishers for the rest of the registration flags.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project A log file arrives as one text column, which is the wrong shape for anything downstream to query. grok turns that column into typed columns by matching a pattern with named captures against every row, so a publisher reading log files parses them on the way in and lands a table with real columns instead of raw lines. The pattern syntax follows the Elasticsearch implementation. For the pattern reference, see the Elasticsearch Grok documentation and the predefined pattern library.
documents.s: Publish data from log files with Grok

documents.t: Log files sit on disk or in object storage, so the connection is a file connection rather than anything grok-specific. A local directory: Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type local-file-in --file conn-logs.yaml Step 2Point base_path at the log directory conn-logs.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.localfile:LocalFileSrcConn spec: base_path: '/var/log/acme' Reading logs out of a bucket instead means s3-file-in or az-file-in here. Nothing else on this page changes: the parsing happens in the publisher body, not in the connection.
Step 3Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name log_src --group sources --conn-file conn-logs.yaml

grok takes three things: the column holding the text, a pattern string, and a schema mapping each capture to an output column and type. A capture is written %{NAME:alias}, where NAME is a predefined pattern such as IPV4, WORD or INT, and alias is the capture name the schema keys on. The full form is %{name:alias:extract:definition}, where definition supplies a regular expression when name is not one of the predefined patterns, and extract is reserved and unused. An Apache access line, parsed into five columns: read_access_logs.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.localfile import LocalFileSrc, SrcFileFormat import tabsdatak.tableframe as tdf import tabsdatak as td PATTERN = ( r"%{IPV4:client_ip} " r"%{USER:ident} " r"%{USER:auth} " r"\[%{HTTPDATE:timestamp}\] " r'"%{WORD:method} ' r'%{URIPATHPARAM:request} ' r'HTTP/%{NUMBER:http_version}" ' r"%{INT:response_code} %{INT:bytes}" ) SCHEMA = { "client_ip": tdf.Column("ip_address", td.String), "method": tdf.Column("http_method", td.String), "response_code": tdf.Column("status_code", td.Int32), "bytes": tdf.Column("response_bytes", td.Int64), "timestamp": tdf.Column("request_time", td.String), } @publisher( source=LocalFileSrc( paths=["access.log"], format=SrcFileFormat.CSV, format_cfg={ SrcFileFormat.CSV: {"has_header": False, "separator": "\\x00"}, }, ), output_tables=["access_logs"], ) def read_access_logs(lines: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if lines is None: return (None,) return (lines[0].grok("column_1", PATTERN, SCHEMA),) The reader has to deliver each log line whole, which is why the CSV options turn the header off and set a separator that does not occur in the text. Without that, a comma inside a log line splits it into columns before grok sees it. The schema keys are capture names and the values are output columns, so a capture the schema leaves out is matched and discarded. That is how ident, auth, request and http_version stay out of the resulting table while still being required by the pattern. Step 4Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll log_src --path read_access_logs.py::read_access_logs
documents.s: Write the pattern and the schema

documents.s: Trigger it and read the table

documents.t: A long pattern makes it easy to write a schema key that no capture produces. grok_fields returns the capture names a pattern generates, in order, so the schema can be written against the real list rather than a guess: check_pattern.py from tabsdatak.expansions.tableframe.features.grok.engine import grok_fields pattern = r"%{WORD:action}-%{INT:year}-%{WORD:action}-%{INT:year}" captures = grok_fields(pattern) # ['action', 'year', 'action[1]', 'year[1]'] Repeated capture names are disambiguated with a bracketed index, starting at 1 for the second occurrence. Both names have to appear in the schema for both captures to reach the table: repeated_captures.py SCHEMA = { "action": tdf.Column("first_name", td.String), "action[1]": tdf.Column("second_name", td.String), "year": tdf.Column("first_year", td.Int64), "year[1]": tdf.Column("second_year", td.Int64), }
documents.s: Finding out what a pattern captures

documents.t: A row the pattern fails to match is kept, with null in every grok column. Nothing is dropped and the run does not fail, so a table with a block of nulls across the parsed columns means the pattern stopped matching rather than that the source went empty. Counting those nulls after a run is the quickest check that a pattern still fits a log format that changed: tdk table data --coll log_src --name access_logs

Every parsed column is null. The pattern does not match the lines. Read one raw line and walk it against the pattern; a changed log format usually breaks at the first literal separator. A schema key raises an error. The key is not a capture the pattern produces. Run grok_fields on the pattern and use the names it returns, including the bracketed ones. Lines arrive already split into several columns. The file reader parsed them as delimited text. Set has_header off and a separator that does not occur in the log lines.

documents.t: function.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc import tabsdatak.api.tableframe as tdf @publisher( source=MySQLSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM employees WHERE emp_no > :emp_no ORDER BY emp_no LIMIT 1000", ], ), output_tables=["employees"], ) def read_employees(employees: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if employees is not None: emp_no = employees.select(tdf.col("emp_no").max()).one()["emp_no"] ctx.set_attr("emp_no", emp_no) return (employees,) queries:list[str]required transactional:booloptional schema_overrides:list[dict | None]optional initial_values:dict[str, Any]optional src_cfg:dict[str, Any]optional trigger_by:list[str] | CronTriggeroptional on_tables:list[DataQuality]optional

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when you call tdk fn trigger. Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when the publisher should poll MySQL on a fixed UTC schedule. The cron mask is standard 5-field crontab syntax, and you can optionally add start and end bounds for a limited run window. This is the right fit when MySQL is the system of record and you want Tabsdata to check it hourly, every night, or on another predictable cadence. read_employees.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc @publisher( source=MySQLSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM employees"], ), output_tables=["employees"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_employees( employees: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (employees,)

Access denied / authentication errors: secrets are read out of the connection file when the collection is created, so an edit made after that point has not reached the server. Re-run tdk connection validate --file conn-mysql.yaml to check the document, then tdk collection update --conn-file conn-mysql.yaml to send the corrected credentials. Check too that the database user has SELECT on every table the queries touch. Connection timeouts: the uri host must be reachable from the Tabsdata server, not from your machine. Driver-level settings (timeouts, charset) go in the connection's conn_cfg. One query fails: the whole run fails and nothing is published. With transactional=True (the default) all queries share one transaction, so a partial set of tables never lands. A run succeeds but a table has no new version: its query matched no rows and the function returned None for that slot, which means keep the current version. See None, and "no new version".

MySQL also offers a stream source, MySQLCdcStreamSrc, with its own connection type mysql-cdc. It streams every insert, update, and delete from the binlog rather than re-running a query. See MySQL CDC.
