Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name world --group sources --conn-file conn-oracle.yaml create validates the document once more, strips the secret values out client-side, and sends both parts to the server. Every publisher registered in world from now on reads through this one connection, and the collection accepts as many publishers as you want to put in it.

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_world.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.oracle import OracleSrc @publisher( source=OracleSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM COUNTRY", "SELECT * FROM CITY", ], ), output_tables=["country", "city"], ) def read_world( country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (country, city) Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll world --path read_world.py::read_world Re-register after every code change. See Publishers for the rest of the registration flags.

Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll world --name read_world Tabsdata runs the queries on the server and writes one versioned table per query. Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll world tdk table data --coll world --name city
documents.s: Trigger it and read the tables

documents.t: Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when you call tdk fn trigger. Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: Oracle publishers can run from a schedule or from changes in another Tabsdata table using trigger_by. 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when Oracle should be polled on a recurring cadence. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.oracle import OracleSrc @publisher( source=OracleSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM INVOICES"], ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices,)

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Postgres connector lets a publisher read data out of a PostgreSQL database and land it in Tabsdata as versioned tables. Each entry in queries is a SELECT statement, and each entry produces one output table. note The PostgreSQL connector needs a database driver that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. See Installing Third-Party Database Drivers for how to declare it during installation. Setting one up takes two files and four commands: a connection document, the collection that carries it, and the publisher registered into that collection.

The connection holds the URI and the credentials, so the publisher holds SQL and nothing about where the database is. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type postgres-sql-in --file conn-postgres.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the URI and the credentials tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.postgres:PostgresSrcConn spec: uri: 'postgres://db.internal:5432/world' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_reader' password: 'secret:example-password' uri:strrequired credentials:UserPasswordrequired entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dict[str, str]optional Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-postgres.yaml

A source collection is created together with its connection, which is why there is no separate collection step ahead of this one and why --conn-file is required rather than optional. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name world --group sources --conn-file conn-postgres.yaml create validates the document once more, strips the secret values out client-side, and sends both parts to the server. Every publisher registered in world from now on reads through this one connection, and the collection accepts as many publishers as you want to put in it. To point the same publisher code at a different database, dev against prod for instance, register it into a second source collection whose connection names a different uri. The code stays untouched.

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_world.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresSrc @publisher( source=PostgresSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM country", "SELECT * FROM city", ], ), output_tables=["country", "city"], ) def read_world( country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (country, city) Each query fills one function argument with a TableFrame, the runtime value behind the TableFrameSpec annotation, or with None when the query matched no rows. The function returns one frame per name in output_tables, in the same order. Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll world --path read_world.py::read_world Re-register after every code change. See Publishers for the rest of the registration flags.

Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll world --name read_world Tabsdata runs the queries on the server and writes one versioned table per query. Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll world tdk table data --coll world --name city
documents.s: Trigger it and read the tables

documents.t: function.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresSrc import tabsdatak.api.tableframe as tdf @publisher( source=PostgresSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000", ], ), output_tables=["invoices"], ) def read_invoices(invoices: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if invoices is not None: last_id = invoices.select(tdf.col("id").max()).one()["id"] ctx.set_attr("last_id", last_id) return (invoices,) queries:list[str]required transactional:booloptional schema_overrides:list[dict | None]optional initial_values:dict[str, Any]optional src_cfg:dict[str, Any]optional trigger_by:list[str] | CronTriggeroptional on_tables:list[DataQuality]optional

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when you call tdk fn trigger. Pass it to have Tabsdata fire the publisher on a clock or on an upstream commit: 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when the publisher should poll PostgreSQL on a fixed UTC schedule. The cron mask is standard 5-field crontab syntax, and you can optionally add start and end bounds for a limited run window. This is the right fit when PostgreSQL is the system of record and you want Tabsdata to check it hourly, every night, or on another predictable cadence. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresSrc @publisher( source=PostgresSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM invoices"], ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices,)

Instead of re-reading a whole table every run, a query can page through it: The :last_id bind takes its value from initial_values on the first run, and from ctx on every run after that. After reading a batch, store the highest id seen with ctx.set_attr("last_id", ...). Values set on ctx are persisted and become the same-named bind's value on the next run, so each trigger continues past the last row read. When the query returns no new rows the slot arrives as None. Returning (None,) keeps the table's current version and leaves the watermark untouched. Compare with a strict > against a unique, monotonically increasing column, a serial key or a commit timestamp, and pair it with ORDER BY and LIMIT so each run reads one bounded, ordered page. With >= the last row of one run is re-read by the next. Queries can use any number of named binds. Seed each one in initial_values and advance whichever ones you set on ctx.

A query that matches no rows fills its slot with None rather than an empty table. Returning None for a table tells Tabsdata to keep the previous version as current instead of committing a new one: read_when_available.py @publisher( source=PostgresSrc(queries=["SELECT * FROM city WHERE 1 = 0"]), output_tables=["city"], ) def read_when_available(city: TableFrameSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (city,)

Access denied or authentication errors. Secrets are read out of the connection file when the collection is created, so an edit made after that point has not reached the server. Re-run tdk connection validate --file conn-postgres.yaml to check the document, then tdk collection update --conn-file conn-postgres.yaml to send the corrected credentials. Check too that the database user has SELECT on every table the queries touch. Connection timeouts. The uri host has to be reachable from the Tabsdata server rather than from your machine. Driver-level settings, timeouts and SSL mode among them, go in the connection's conn_cfg. One query fails. The whole run fails and nothing is published. With transactional=True, the default, all queries share one transaction, so a partial set of tables never lands. A run succeeds but a table has no new version. Its query matched no rows and the function returned None for that slot, which means keep the current version.

PostgreSQL also offers a stream source, PostgresCdcStreamSrc, with its own connection type postgres-cdc. It streams every insert, update and delete from the logical replication stream rather than re-running a query. See PostgreSQL CDC.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project A Salesforce publisher runs SOQL queries against a Salesforce org and lands each result as a versioned table. Each entry in queries produces one output table, so the query list and the table list line up position by position. The connector ships separately from the core package: pip install 'tabsdata[salesforce]'
documents.s: Publish data from a Salesforce SOQL query

documents.t: The connection holds the org credentials: a username, a password, and a security token. The username is the Salesforce username rather than the email address on the account, which is the mistake that most often produces an authentication failure on a first attempt. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type salesforce-sosql-in --file conn-salesforce.yaml Step 2Fill in the username, password, and security token conn-salesforce.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.salesforce:SalesforceSrcConn spec: credentials: kind: salesforceTokenCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:SalesforceToken spec: username: 'secret:integration@acme.com' password: 'secret:example-password' security_token: 'secret:exampleSecurityToken00' To find the security token, open View Profile in Salesforce, go to Settings, and choose Reset My Security Token. Salesforce mails the new token and invalidates the old one, so reset it only when you are ready to update the connection. instance_url is optional and belongs on the connection when one set of credentials maps to more than one org. Left out, the instance is inferred from the username and password. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-salesforce.yaml

A source collection is created together with its connection, which is why --conn-file is required rather than optional. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name sf_src --group sources --conn-file conn-salesforce.yaml

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_sales.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceSrc @publisher( source=SalesforceSrc( queries=[ "SELECT Id, AccountId, FirstName, LastName, Email, SystemModStamp " "FROM Contact WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified", "SELECT Name, Type, SystemModStamp " "FROM Account WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified", ], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000+0000", ), output_tables=["contacts", "accounts"], ) def read_sales( contacts: TableFramesSpec, accounts: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (contacts[0], accounts[0]) Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sf_src --path read_sales.py::read_sales Re-register after every code change.
Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll sf_src --name read_sales Step 8Inspect the resulting tables tdk table list --coll sf_src tdk table data --coll sf_src --name contacts
documents.s: Trigger it and read the tables

documents.t: Every Salesforce object carries a SystemModStamp column, and Tabsdata reads it to publish only the rows that changed since the previous run. Two things have to be true for that to work: SystemModStamp appears in the SELECT list, and the WHERE clause compares it against the $lastModified placeholder. On the first run $lastModified takes the value of initial_last_modified. On every later run it takes the highest SystemModStamp seen so far, so each trigger reads forward from where the last one stopped. Deletions are invisible to that comparison, because a deleted row stops appearing rather than getting a newer timestamp. Set include_deleted to True to read deleted records too, which is what makes an incremental load able to tell that a row went away.

Parameter Required What it does queries yes SOQL queries, one per output table, in order initial_last_modified no Starting timestamp for the first incremental run include_deleted no Reads deleted records as well. Defaults to False instance_url no Disambiguates the org when the credentials map to several version no Salesforce API version. Defaults to the latest

A query that returns no rows fills its slot with None rather than an empty frame. Returning None for a table tells Tabsdata to keep the previous version as current instead of committing a new one, which is the usual outcome of an incremental run with nothing new to read: read_when_available.py @publisher( source=SalesforceSrc( queries=["SELECT Id, Email, SystemModStamp FROM Contact " "WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified"], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000+0000", ), output_tables=["contacts"], ) def read_when_available(contacts: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: if contacts is None: return (None,) return (contacts[0],)

Authentication fails. Check that the username is the Salesforce username and not the email address, and that the security token matches the current password. Resetting either one invalidates the token. Every run re-reads everything. The query is missing $lastModified in its WHERE clause, or SystemModStamp is missing from the SELECT list. Both are required for the incremental read. Rows disappear from the source but stay in the table. include_deleted defaults to False, so deletions are not read at all. Wrong org. One set of credentials that maps to several orgs needs instance_url on the connection to pick between them.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project A Salesforce Reports publisher reads a report that already exists in Salesforce, rather than a query you write, and lands its rows as a versioned table. The report's own definition decides which columns come back, so the publisher names the report and adds filters instead of selecting columns. The connector ships separately from the core package: pip install 'tabsdata[salesforce]'

The connection holds the org credentials: a username, a password, and a security token. The username is the Salesforce username rather than the email address on the account. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type salesforce-report-in --file conn-sf-report.yaml Step 2Fill in the username, password, and security token conn-sf-report.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.salesforce:SalesforceReportSrcConn spec: credentials: kind: salesforceTokenCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:SalesforceToken spec: username: 'secret:integration@acme.com' password: 'secret:example-password' security_token: 'secret:exampleSecurityToken00' To find the security token, open View Profile in Salesforce, go to Settings, and choose Reset My Security Token. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-sf-report.yaml
Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name sf_reports --group sources --conn-file conn-sf-report.yaml

Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_contacts.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceReportSrc @publisher( source=SalesforceReportSrc( report=["contacts"], column_name_strategy="columnName", filter=[ ("COUNTRY", "equals", "USA"), ("COUNTRY", "equals", "France"), ], filter_logic="1 or 2", initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000+0000", ), output_tables=["contacts"], ) def read_contacts(contacts: TableFramesSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (contacts[0],) Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sf_reports --path read_contacts.py::read_contacts
Step 7Trigger the publisher tdk fn trigger --coll sf_reports --name read_contacts Step 8Inspect the resulting table tdk table list --coll sf_reports tdk table data --coll sf_reports --name contacts
documents.s: Trigger it and read the table

documents.t: report takes one report or a list of them, referenced by id or by name. Which of the two is meant is inferred from the value, and find_report_by states it outright when the inference would guess wrong. A report referenced by name uses what Salesforce calls the report unique name, also shown as the developer name, rather than the label displayed in the UI. column_name_strategy decides where the output column names come from. A Salesforce report carries both a columnName and a label for every column: CREATED_ALIAS against alias, for instance. The choice sets the column names in the resulting Tabsdata table, and it also sets the names the filters have to use, so a filter written against labels breaks when the strategy is columnName.
documents.s: Naming a report, and naming its columns

documents.t: Each filter is a tuple of a column, an operator, and a value, in the form Salesforce report queries already use. More than one filter goes in a list. filter_logic states how those filters combine, referring to them by position: the first filter in the list is 1, the second is 2, and so on. "1 or 2" accepts a row matching either, and "1 or (2 and 3)" groups them. Without filter_logic, the filters carry no stated relationship between them.

initial_last_modified sets where the first run starts, as a string in Salesforce datetime format with the timezone included. last_modified_column names the column the comparison runs against, and that column has to be in the report for the read to work. It defaults to None, which reads the whole report on every run.

Parameter Required What it does report yes One report or a list, by id or by name column_name_strategy yes columnName or label, setting output column names find_report_by no id or name, when the reference is ambiguous filter no Tuples of column, operator, value filter_logic no How the filters combine, by position initial_last_modified no Starting timestamp for the first incremental run last_modified_column no Report column driving the incremental read instance_url no Disambiguates the org when the credentials map to several

A filter matches nothing. Filters use whichever names column_name_strategy selected, so a filter written against alias fails under columnName and needs CREATED_ALIAS instead. The report is not found by name. Salesforce matches the report unique name, not the label in the UI. Set find_report_by to name and pass the unique name, or reference the report by id. Every run re-reads the whole report. last_modified_column is unset, or the column it names is missing from the report definition.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Subscribe data to Amazon S3 connector lets a subscriber write Tabsdata tables out to Subscribe data to Amazon S3. Each entry in paths takes one input table, in order, and writes it as an object at that path. Setting one up takes two files and four commands: a connection document, the destination collection that carries it, and the subscriber registered into that collection.

The connection holds the bucket or container, the credentials, and the optional base_path that destination paths resolve against. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type s3-file-out --file conn-s3.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the destination and the credentials tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3DestConn spec: bucket: 'acme-exports' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-s3.yaml

A destination collection is created together with its connection, which is why --conn-file is required rather than optional, and why the group is destinations rather than sources. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name exports --group destinations --conn-file conn-s3.yaml Every subscriber registered in exports from now on writes through this one connection. Changing environments means swapping the connection rather than editing the Python file.

Step 5Build the subscriber file locally write_files.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Dest @subscriber( destination=S3Dest( paths=["departments_\${EXEC_PLAN_TS}.parquet", "employees_\${EXEC_PLAN_TS}.parquet"], ), input_tables=["hr/departments", "hr/employees"], ) def write_files( departments: TableFrameSpec, employees: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (departments, employees) Input tables are referenced as collection/table, since a subscriber reads from collections other than its own. A subscriber declares no output_tables: it returns one frame per destination slot, and returning None for a slot writes nothing. Step 6Register the subscriber into the collection tdk fn register --coll exports --path write_files.py::write_files Re-register after every code change. See Subscribers for the rest of the registration flags.
Step 7Run the subscriber tdk fn trigger --coll exports --name write_files Tabsdata writes one object per path on the server. Step 8Verify the data arrived aws s3 ls s3://acme-exports/sales/

The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-bigquery.yaml

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The ClickHouse connector is destination-only. It stages Parquet files in cloud storage and then loads them through ClickHouse table functions such as s3() or azureBlobStorage(). The connector currently supports S3, Azure Blob, and GCS staging. Each entry in tables takes one input table, in order, and writes it to that destination table. The connector ships separately from the core package: pip install 'tabsdata[clickhouse]'

The connection holds the server address, the credentials, and a staging block naming the cloud storage the load goes through. Rows reach ClickHouse as Parquet staged in that location rather than row by row, so the staging credentials have to be writable as well as readable. documents.s: Trigger it and check the destination

documents.t: Without an explicit trigger_by, a subscriber runs whenever any of its input tables receives a new commit. Add trigger_by=[...] only when you need tighter control over which upstream table changes should schedule the export.

If an input table dependency does not exist for a run, the subscriber can receive None instead of a frame. Returning None means there is nothing to write for that output slot, which avoids unnecessary duplicate writes. For schema evolution, if_table_exists="replace" is the most forgiving option because it rebuilds the destination table from the latest frame. With "append", PostgreSQL keeps the existing schema, so column additions, removals, or type changes can fail unless your function keeps the exported shape stable.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The StarRocks connector is destination-only. It stages Parquet files in cloud storage and then loads them through the native FILES() path in StarRocks. Each entry in tables takes one input table, in order, and writes it to that destination table. The connector ships separately from the core package: pip install 'tabsdata[starrocks]'

The connection holds the server address, the credentials, and a staging block naming the cloud storage the load goes through. Rows reach StarRocks as Parquet staged in that location rather than row by row, so the staging credentials have to be writable as well as readable. documents.t: The target tables must already exist. StarRocks requires physical layout such as key definitions and distribution strategy, so the connector does not create missing tables for you. The connection supports S3, Azure Blob, or GCS staging. GCS staging requires both service-account JSON for uploads and HMAC credentials so StarRocks can read the staged files through the S3-compatible endpoint. schema_evolution supports "strict" and "iceberg".
Aggregate data to compute summary statistics.

count()len()sum()mean()median()min()max()first()last()n_unique() Non-null count count.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return tf.select(col("id").count()) events id 1 null 3 3 rows result id 2 1 row

Use group_by() to aggregate by groups: Single Column GroupingMulti-Column GroupingExpression-based Grouping Group rows by unique values within a single column agg.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.group_by("category").agg( col("sales").sum().alias("total_sales"), col("quantity").mean().alias("avg_quantity") ) return result sales category sales quantity tools 100 4 toys 40 2 tools 60 6 3 rows result category total_sales avg_quantity tools 160 5 toys 40 2 2 rows

For simple aggregations: count()sum()mean()min()max() Count per group count.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.group_by("category").count() return result sales category sales tools 100 toys 40 tools 60 3 rows result category sales tools 2 toys 1 2 rows

Assign ranks to values: averageminmaxdenseordinalrandom The average of the ranks that would have been assigned to all the tied values is assigned to each value. rank.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.with_columns(col("score").rank(method="average").alias("avg_rank")) return result results player score Ada 7 Bo 5 Cy 7 3 rows result player score avg_rank Ada 7 2.5 Bo 5 1 Cy 7 2.5 3 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.

For floating-point columns: drop_nans() 1drop_nans() 2fill_nan() 1fill_nan() 2 Drop rows with NaN values drop_nans.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.drop_nans() return result readings id ratio percentage 1 0.5 90 2 NaN 80 3 0.9 NaN 3 rows result id ratio percentage 1 0.5 90 1 row

sort() 1sort() 2sort() 3sort() 4 Sort by single column (ascending) sort.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.sort("date") return result events category date value b 2024-03-01 2 a 2024-01-15 9 a 2024-05-20 5 3 rows result category date value a 2024-01-15 9 b 2024-03-01 2 a 2024-05-20 5 3 rows

cast() 1cast() 2cast() 3cast() 4to_date()to_datetime()to_time()to_integer()to_string() Cast expression type cast.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes import Int64 @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("id").cast(Int64) return tf.with_columns(expr) records idString 1 2 2 rows result idInt64 1 2 2 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.
Combine rows from two or more Tabsdata Tables. A transformer declares one input_tables entry per table and takes a parameter for each.

concat() stacks TableFrames by appending their rows. how decides what happens when the inputs do not line up: verticalvertical_relaxeddiagonaldiagonal_relaxed The default, so it can be left off. Every input must share the same columns and the same types. concat.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @transformer( input_tables=["sales_east", "sales_west"], output_tables=["sales_all"], ) def transform(east: TableFrameSpec, west: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = concat([east, west]) return result sales_east region month amount east jan 10 east feb 20 2 rows sales_west region month amount west jan 30 west feb 40 2 rows sales_all region month amount east jan 10 east feb 20 west jan 30 west feb 40 4 rows note None entries in the list are skipped. A list that is None, empty, or empty once the None entries are dropped makes concat() return None, which leaves the output table on its current version instead of committing a new one. See concat for the full signature.
While TableFrames are typically received as input in publishers and transformers, you can also create them programmatically for testing or data generation purposes.

Use TableFrame.from_dict() to create a TableFrame from a Python dictionary: transform.py from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame data = { "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"], "age": [25, 30, 35], "city": ["New York", "London", "Paris"] } tf = TableFrame.from_dict(data)

Convert a Pandas DataFrame to a TableFrame: transform.py import pandas as pd from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame df = pd.DataFrame({ "product": ["Widget", "Gadget"], "price": [19.99, 29.99] }) tf = TableFrame.from_pandas(df)

Convert from Polars LazyFrame or DataFrame: transform.py import polars as pl from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame # From Polars LazyFrame lf = pl.LazyFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [4, 5, 6]}) tf = TableFrame.from_polars(lf) # From Polars DataFrame pdf = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [4, 5, 6]}) tf = TableFrame.from_polars(pdf)

Export TableFrames to other formats: transform.py # To dictionary data_dict = tf.to_dict() # To Pandas DataFrame pandas_df = tf.to_pandas() # To Polars DataFrame polars_df = tf.to_polars_df() # To Polars LazyFrame polars_lf = tf.to_polars_lf() See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.

to_string()strftime()epoch()timestamp() Format as string to_string.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("date").dt.to_string("%Y-%m-%d") return tf.with_columns(expr) events dateDate 2024-03-15 2024-11-01 2 rows result dateString 2024-03-15 2024-11-01 2 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.
Filter operations allow you to select rows based on conditions.

Use filter() with boolean expressions: greater thanequalsnot equals Simple comparison filter.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.filter(col("age") > 18) return result persons name age Ada 25 Bo 17 Cy 30 3 rows result name age Ada 25 Cy 30 2 rows

Combine multiple conditions using logical operators: AND (bitwise)and (logical)OR (bitwise)OR (logical)NOT (Bitwise)NOT (logical)XOR AND conditions (two syntaxes) filter.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.filter((col("age") > 18) & (col("age") < 65)) return result persons name age Ada 25 Bo 17 Cy 70 3 rows result name age Ada 25 1 row

is_between()is_in()is_not_null()is_null()is_not_nan() Between (inclusive) is_between.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.filter(col("price").is_between(10.0, 100.0)) return result items item price widget 9.5 gadget 42 anvil 250 3 rows result item price gadget 42 1 row

Access metadata about your TableFrame.

transform.py # Get column data types dtypes = tf.dtypes # Check if columns exist tf.has_cols("column_name") tf.has_cols(["col1", "col2"]) # Assert columns exist (raises error if not) tf.assert_has_cols(["required_col1", "required_col2"]) # Compare schemas tf.has_same_schema(other_tf)
transform.py # Check if TableFrame is empty tf.is_empty() # Create an empty TableFrame with same schema empty_tf = tf.empty() # Clear all rows cleared_tf = tf.clear()

For debugging and optimization: transform.py # Get query plan explanation plan = tf.explain() print(plan) # Visualize query graph tf.show_graph() See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.

A transformer reads one or more Tabsdata Tables and writes new Tabsdata Tables. Joining two of them is the most common case: declare both under input_tables and the function takes a parameter for each. See Transformers for the anatomy of a transformer Function. Every block below joins the same two tables. orders has three rows and customers has three, overlapping on two customer_id values: o3 points at c9, which no customer has, and c3 has no order. What a join does with those two rows is the whole difference between the types.

Set the type with how. Every one of these joins on customer_id: innerleftrightfullsemianti Only the rows that match on both sides. The default. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "customers"], output_tables=["order_names"], ) def transform(orders: TableFrameSpec, customers: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = orders.join(customers, on="customer_id") return result orders order_id customer_id amount o1 c1 10 o2 c2 20 o3 c9 5 3 rows customers customer_id name c1 Ada c2 Grace c3 Cy 3 rows order_names order_id customer_id amount name o1 c1 10 Ada o2 c2 20 Grace 2 rows

A key can span several columns, and the two sides can name them differently: on=[...]left_on / right_on One key spanning several columns. A row matches only when every column agrees. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["visits", "targets"], output_tables=["visits_vs_target"], ) def transform(visits: TableFrameSpec, targets: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = visits.join(targets, on=["customer_id", "date"]) return result visits customer_id date spend c1 mon 10 c2 mon 7 c1 tue 4 3 rows targets customer_id date target c1 mon 12 c2 mon 5 2 rows visits_vs_target customer_id date spend target c1 mon 10 12 c2 mon 7 5 2 rows

When both tables carry a column of the same name, the right-hand one needs a new name: Renames the right-hand copy of every colliding column. The join key stays single. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "returns"], output_tables=["orders_returns"], ) def transform(orders: TableFrameSpec, returns: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = orders.join(returns, on="id", suffix="_return") return result orders id amount o1 10 o2 20 2 rows returns id amount o1 4 o2 20 2 rows orders_returns id amount amount_return o1 10 4 o2 20 20 2 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.
Mathematical and numeric operations on columns.

+-*/add()sub()mul()truediv()mod() Basic arithmetic add.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("price") + 10 return tf.with_columns(expr) orders price 100 40 2 rows result price 110 50 2 rows

round()round_sig_figs()floor()ceil()clip() Round to 2 decimal places round.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("price").round(2) # Round to 2 decimal places return tf.with_columns(expr) items item price widget 19.9876 gadget 4.201 2 rows result item price widget 19.99 gadget 4.2 2 rows

abs()sign()neg()pow()sqrt()cbrt()log()log10()log1p()exp() Absolute value and sign abs.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("change").abs() return tf.with_columns(expr) readings change -4.5 2 2 rows result change 4.5 2 2 rows

sin()cos()tan()cot()arcsin()arccos()arctan()sinh()cosh()tanh()radians()degrees() Basic trig functions sin.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("angle").sin() return tf.with_columns(expr) readings angle 0 1 2 rows result angle 0 0.8415 2 rows

diff() 1diff() 2 Difference from previous row diff.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("value").diff() # Difference from previous row return tf.with_columns(expr) readings value 10 13 9 3 rows result value null 3 -4 3 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.
Extract specific data patterns from tables.

Pivot unique values into columns: Extract unique values from a column as separate columns extract_as_columns.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.extract_as_columns( column="metric_name", value_column="metric_value" ) return result metrics host metric_name metric_value web1 cpu 80 web1 mem 60 web2 cpu 35 web2 mem 45 4 rows result host cpu mem web1 80 60 web2 35 45 2 rows

Unpivot columns into rows: Melt multiple columns into rows extract_as_rows.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.extract_as_rows( columns=["jan_sales", "feb_sales", "mar_sales"], variable_name="month", value_name="sales" ) return result sales region jan_sales feb_sales mar_sales east 10 20 30 1 row result region month sales east jan_sales 10 east feb_sales 20 east mar_sales 30 3 rows

Flatten nested structures: Expands struct fields to columns unnest.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.unnest("address") # Expands struct fields to columns return result people name address Ada {city: Austin, zip: 78701} Grace {city: Arlington, zip: 22201} 2 rows result name city zip Ada Austin 78701 Grace Arlington 22201 2 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.
Projection operations allow you to select, transform, and reshape columns in your data.

Use select() to choose specific columns. Multiple syntax forms are supported: select(*Expr)select(*str)select(*list[*str]) Select a column using col() expressions select.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.select(col("first_name"), col("last_name")) return result people first_name last_name age Ada Lovelace 36 Grace Hopper 45 2 rows result first_name last_name Ada Lovelace Grace Hopper 2 rows

Tabsdata provides powerful selectors to dynamically select columns by type or pattern: By Data Type: numeric()string()temporal()by_dtype() Select all numeric columns numeric.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer import tabsdatak.tableframe.selectors as cs @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.select(cs.numeric()) return result records idInt64 priceFloat64 nameString createdDate 1 9.99 widget 2024-03-15 2 4.50 gadget 2024-11-01 2 rows result idInt64 priceFloat64 1 9.99 2 4.50 2 rows By Pattern: starts_with()ends_with()contains()matches() Select columns starting with a prefix starts_with.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer import tabsdatak.tableframe.selectors as cs @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.select(cs.starts_with("customer_")) return result orders customer_id customer_name price amount_1 note_id c1 Ada 10 5 n1 c2 Grace 20 7 n2 2 rows result customer_id customer_name c1 Ada c2 Grace 2 rows By Position: first()last()by_index() Select first N columns first.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer import tabsdatak.tableframe.selectors as cs @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.select(cs.first(3)) return result orders customer_id customer_name price amount_1 note_id c1 Ada 10 5 n1 c2 Grace 20 7 n2 2 rows result customer_id customer_name price c1 Ada 10 c2 Grace 20 2 rows Excluding Columns: exclude()Arithmetical Expression Select all columns except specific ones exclude.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer import tabsdatak.tableframe.selectors as cs @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.select(cs.exclude("internal_id", "metadata")) return result records id internal_id metadata 1 x1 seed 2 x2 import 2 rows result id 1 2 2 rows

Use with_columns() to add new columns or modify existing ones without dropping other columns: Add new columns, or replace exisitng ones. with_columns.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col, lit @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.with_columns( # Add a new calculated column (col("price") * col("quantity")).alias("total"), # Modify an existing column col("name").str.to_uppercase().alias("name"), # Add a literal value column lit("USD").alias("currency") ) return result orders name price quantity widget 10 3 gadget 4 2 2 rows result name price quantity total currency WIDGET 10 3 30 USD GADGET 4 2 8 USD 2 rows

Use drop() to remove columns: drop(str)drop(*str)Using Selectors Drop a single column using the column name drop.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.drop("temporary_column") return result records id temporary_column 1 tmp 2 tmp 2 rows result id 1 2 2 rows

Use rename() to change column names: Give columns new names, leaving their values untouched. rename.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.rename({ "old_name": "new_name", "customer_id": "cust_id" }) return result records old_name customer_id Ada c1 Grace c2 2 rows result new_name cust_id Ada c1 Grace c2 2 rows

Use alias() on expressions to name computed columns: Keep only the listed expressions, in the order given. select.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.select( (col("first_name") + " " + col("last_name")).alias("full_name"), (col("price") * 1.1).alias("price_with_tax") ) return result orders first_name last_name price Ada Lovelace 10 Grace Hopper 20 2 rows result full_name price_with_tax Ada Lovelace 11 Grace Hopper 22 2 rows

Create constant value columns: Add literal value columns with_columns.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import lit @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.with_columns( lit(1).alias("version"), lit("active").alias("status"), lit(True).alias("is_valid"), lit(3.14159).alias("pi") ) return result records id 1 2 2 rows result id version status is_valid pi 1 1 active true 3.14159 2 1 active true 3.14159 2 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.
The .str namespace provides comprehensive string manipulation functions.

to_uppercase()to_lowercase()to_titlecase() Upper-case every character. to_uppercase.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("name").str.to_uppercase() return tf.with_columns(expr) persons name age ada Lovelace 36 Grace HOPPER 45 2 rows result name age ADA LOVELACE 36 GRACE HOPPER 45 2 rows

ends_with()starts_with()contains() 1contains_any()contains() 2 Check if string starts/ends with pattern ends_with.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("email").str.ends_with("@example.com") return tf.with_columns(expr) contacts email ada@example.com bo@other.org 2 rows result email True False 2 rows

extract()replace()replace_all()replace_many() Extract using regex groups extract.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("email").str.extract(r"@(\w+)\.", group_index=1) return tf.with_columns(expr) contacts email ada@example.com bo@other.org 2 rows result email example other 2 rows

strip_chars()strip_chars_start()strip_chars_end()strip_prefix()strip_suffix()pad_start()pad_end()zfill()head()tail()slice()reverse() Both sides strip_chars.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("name").str.strip_chars() # Both sides return tf.with_columns(expr) people name Ada Grace 2 rows result name Ada Grace 2 rows

len_chars()len_bytes()find()count_matches() Character count len_chars.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("description").str.len_chars() # Character count return tf.with_columns(expr) tickets description disk failure ok 2 rows result description 12 2 2 rows

Parse semi-structured text using Grok patterns: Parse Apache log format grok.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.grok( "log_line", r"%{IP:client_ip} - - \[%{HTTPDATE:timestamp}\] \"%{WORD:method} %{URIPATHPARAM:path}\"" ) return result access log_line 10.0.0.1 - - [12/Mar/2024:09:15:00 +0000] "GET /users" 1 row result log_line client_ip timestamp method path 10.0.0.1 - - [12/Mar/2024:09:15:00 +0000] "GET /users" 10.0.0.1 12/Mar/2024:09:15:00 +0000 GET /users 1 row See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.

Before you begin Create a Project A CDC stream source reads a database's replication log and emits one Tabsdata table per tracked table. Every insert, update, and delete arrives, rather than whatever a SELECT happens to see when it runs. Three databases have a CDC source, each with its own connection type: Connection type Database Class mysql-cdc MySQL MySQLCdcStreamSrc postgres-cdc PostgreSQL PostgresCdcStreamSrc db2-cdc IBM Db2 Db2CdcStreamSrc What runs the publisher is a rollover rather than a clock or an upstream commit. The stream worker consumes the log continuously, and when a threshold trips it writes the buffer out and hands the batch to the publisher, which de-duplicates and offset-filters the rows before ingesting them. @stream_publisher takes no trigger_by. Step 1Create the connection tdk connection template --type mysql-cdc --file conn-cdc.yaml Fill in the URI, the credentials, and the tables list, then create the collection: tdk collection create \ --name inventory \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-cdc.yaml All three CDC types register with direction stream-src, which maps to the sources group. Step 2Write the stream publisher read_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLCdcStreamSrc @stream_publisher( source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc( tables=["shop.products", "shop.stock"], start_from="tail", ), flush_interval_mins=5, output_tables=["products", "stock"], ) def read_changes( products: TableFramesSpec, stock: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFramesSpec, TableFramesSpec]: return (products, stock) One output table per tracked table, in order, and one TableFramesSpec parameter per slot. The function must not declare a ctx parameter: it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. Step 3Register it tdk fn register \ --coll inventory \ --path read_changes.py::read_changes Registration starts the stream worker, which begins consuming the log.
documents.s: Trigger off CDC in an SQL Database

documents.t: start_from decides what the worker reads first. For PostgreSQL, "head" starts at the oldest retained WAL, "tail" starts at the current LSN, and an LsnPosition starts at a position you name. Starting at the tail skips the history and streams only what arrives from now on.

PostgreSQL logical replication is slot-based, so its connection carries fields the other two do not: Field Purpose replication_slot The slot name, required replication_slot_behavior "reuse" (default) or "create" publication_name Optional publication to read from columns_format "columns" (default), "struct", or "map" flatten_columns Defaults to True

flush_interval_mins is a fallback ceiling, minimum 1 whole minute. The connector's own thresholds in src_cfg cover buffer size and polling cadence, and whichever threshold trips first closes the batch, so the connector's window is usually the one that fires.

MySQL and PostgreSQL CDC both need a database driver that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. Declare it during installation, as described in Installing Third-Party Database Drivers. Adding it later means re-running the installation.
Trigger off a Kafka Stream covers the fourth stream source, which follows the same rollover model against a topic. See Stage Triggers for how a batch closes and becomes a run.

Before you begin Create a Project A CronTrigger runs a function at fixed times whether or not any upstream data changed. It is the right trigger for a publisher, which has nothing inside Tabsdata to signal that its external system has new rows. Tabsdata reads every crontab schedule in UTC. Step 1Add a CronTrigger to the function read_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import CronTrigger, TableFrameSpec, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc @publisher( source=MySQLSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM orders"], ), output_tables=["orders"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders "0 * * * *" fires at the top of every hour. The mask is standard 5-field crontab syntax, Minute Hour Day Month Day-of-Week, with minute precision. Extensions like @hourly and @daily are not supported. Mask When it runs 0,30 * * * * Every 30 minutes, on the hour and at minute 30 0 0 * * * Daily at 00:00 UTC 0 22 * * FRI Fridays at 22:00 UTC Step 2Register the function tdk fn register \ --coll sales \ --path read_orders.py::read_orders The schedule starts from the moment registration succeeds. Re-register with --update after any change to the mask. Step 3Confirm the schedule took tdk fn get --coll sales --name read_orders

start and end limit when the mask applies. Both take a timezone-aware Python datetime or an ISO 8601 string in UTC: trigger_by=CronTrigger( "0 * * * *", start="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", end="2026-04-01T00:00:00Z", ) Omit them and the mask applies indefinitely from registration.
documents.s: Bounding the schedule to a window

documents.t: A cron schedule only fires while its function is enabled, so pausing one is a matter of disabling the function rather than editing the mask: tdk fn disable --coll sales --name read_orders tdk fn enable --coll sales --name read_orders A disabled function keeps its registration and its mask, and Tabsdata ignores the mask until it is enabled again. Register a function --disabled to add it without starting its schedule.

A cron trigger fires on a clock regardless of upstream state. To run a function because data actually arrived, see Trigger a Function from a Table Commit. See Cron Triggers for how the trigger behaves.

Before you begin Create a Project A Kafka stream source consumes one topic continuously and emits a single Tabsdata table named after that topic. What runs the publisher is neither a clock nor an upstream commit but a rollover: the stream worker buffers messages, and when a rollover threshold trips it writes the buffer out as parquet and hands the batch to the publisher to ingest. @stream_publisher therefore takes no trigger_by at all. Step 1Create the connection tdk connection template --type kafka-topic-in --file conn-kafka.yaml Fill in the bootstrap servers, then create the collection with it: tdk collection create \ --name events \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-kafka.yaml servers is the only required field. credentials is optional, so a broker that takes SASL gets a UserPassword block here and a broker without authentication gets none. The topic is not a connection field: it belongs to the source in the function, along with the message format and schema. A Kafka connection registers with direction stream-src, which maps to the sources group like a plain source does. Step 2Write the stream publisher read_clicks.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.kafka import KafkaStreamSrc CLICK_SCHEMA = """ { "type": "record", "name": "Click", "fields": [ {"name": "user_id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "url", "type": "string"}, {"name": "ts", "type": "long"} ] } """ @stream_publisher( source=KafkaStreamSrc( topic="clicks", data_format="json", schema=CLICK_SCHEMA, ), flush_interval_mins=5, output_tables=["clicks"], ) def read_clicks(clicks: TableFramesSpec) -> TableFramesSpec: return clicks The output table takes the topic's name, and there is always exactly one. schema is required, and in schema-registry mode it is cross-checked against the registry. The function takes one TableFramesSpec per source slot, always in array mode, and must not declare a ctx parameter: it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction, so no transaction context exists at the call boundary. Step 3Register it tdk fn register \ --coll events \ --path read_clicks.py::read_clicks Registration starts the stream worker. It consumes continuously from that point.

Rollover fires on whichever threshold trips first, the connector's own or the decorator's fallback. Kafka takes min(time_rollover_secs, flush_interval_mins * 60), so flush_interval_mins is a ceiling and the connector's window is usually the one that fires. Set the connector's thresholds in src_cfg: Key Closes the batch when kafka.time_rollover_seconds That many seconds have passed kafka.size_rollover_mb The buffer reaches that size kafka.messages_rollover That many messages have accumulated flush_interval_mins takes whole minutes, minimum 1.
Set dlq_topic on the source and Kafka messages that cannot be deserialized are routed there instead of failing the batch.

Trigger off CDC in an SQL Database covers the other three stream sources, which follow the same rollover model against a database log. See Stage Triggers for how a batch closes and becomes a run, and Kafka for the full connector setup.

Before you begin Create a Project tdk fn trigger runs a registered function on demand. Any function can be triggered this way, including one that already carries a trigger_by schedule, so a manual trigger is how you test a function before trusting it to a cron mask. A publisher with no trigger_by runs only when triggered manually. That is the default for publishers, since nothing upstream inside Tabsdata can signal that an external system has new data. Step 1Trigger the function tdk fn trigger \ --coll sales \ --name read_orders The command waits for the plan to finish and reports each function as it completes. Pass --detach to return immediately instead. Step 2Check what the run produced tdk table list --coll sales tdk table data --coll sales --name orders

A trigger does not run one function in isolation. Tabsdata builds an execution plan covering every function downstream of the one you named, and runs them in dependency order: a transformer reading the publisher's output runs next, then a subscriber reading that transformer's output. Nothing commits unless every function in the plan succeeds. Name the plan to make it easier to find afterward: tdk fn trigger \ --coll sales \ --name read_orders \ --plan-name nightly-backfill
documents.s: Triggering runs more than one function

documents.t: tdk fnrun list --coll sales --fn read_orders The listing carries each run's id, which is what the log and recovery commands take: tdk fnrun logs --fnrun <run_id> tdk fnrun recover --fnrun <run_id> recover resumes the plan a failed run belongs to rather than starting a new one.

Automate it. Schedule a Cron Trigger runs the function on a clock, and Trigger a Function from a Table Commit runs it when an upstream table gets new data. See Manual Triggers for how the trigger behaves, and tdk fn trigger for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project A table trigger runs a function whenever a table it watches receives a new commit. This is how a pipeline advances on its own: a publisher lands data, the transformer watching that table runs, and the subscriber watching the transformer's output runs after it. Transformers and subscribers already work this way without being told to. Omit trigger_by and a commit to any of the function's input tables triggers it. trigger_by is for the two cases the default does not cover: triggering off fewer tables than the function reads, and triggering off tables it does not read at all. Step 1Write the function against its input tables summarize.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["orders"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], ) def summarize(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders.group_by("region").agg(col("amount").sum()) With no trigger_by, a commit to orders runs this transformer. Step 2Register it tdk fn register \ --coll sales \ --path summarize.py::summarize Step 3Trigger the upstream function and watch the chain tdk fn trigger --coll sales --name read_orders The publisher commits orders, which triggers summarize in the same execution plan. Both appear in the run listing: tdk fnrun list --coll sales
documents.s: Trigger a Function from a Table Commit

documents.t: A commit to any input table triggers the function, and trigger_by narrows that set: @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "regions"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], trigger_by=["orders"], ) regions is still read on every run and still supplies its current data. It no longer starts one, which suits a lookup table whose edits do not warrant recomputing the summary. This is not about avoiding duplicate runs. A plan that commits both orders and regions runs this transformer once either way, because the plan covers every downstream function and orders them by dependency rather than firing one run per committed table.

trigger_by accepts tables that are not inputs at all, which is how a function runs in response to something it does not consume. input_tables and trigger_by are two independent lists — one controls what the function reads, the other what starts it, and neither has to be a subset of the other: @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "regions"], output_tables=["orders_by_region"], trigger_by=["orders", "ops/refresh_signal"], ) def summarize(orders: TableFrameSpec, regions: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders.group_by("region").agg(col("amount").sum()) regions is read on every run but never starts one, since it is absent from trigger_by. ops/refresh_signal starts a run despite never being read, since it is absent from input_tables. A commit to ops/refresh_signal runs the transformer even though it reads nothing from that table. A publisher uses the same mechanism: it has no input_tables at all, so a table reference in trigger_by is the only way a Tabsdata commit can start it. Reference a table outside the function's own collection as collection/table. Cross-collection references work within one project. A reference to a table in another project surfaces as Dependency table '<x>' does not exist, because row-level security hides it rather than reporting it as forbidden.
documents.s: Triggering off a table the function does not read

documents.t: An empty list disables it, leaving the function manual-only: trigger_by=[]

A publisher writing three tables commits all three on every run, whether or not the rows in a given table differ from last time, and every commit triggers whatever watches that table. A run that returns None for a table is the exception: that keeps the current version instead of committing a new one, so nothing downstream fires.
documents.s: A commit does not mean the data changed

documents.t: Schedule a Cron Trigger to run a function on a clock instead, which is what a publisher usually needs. See Table Commit Triggers for how the trigger behaves.

Tabsdata is a distributed, horizontally scalable system that runs on a Kubernetes cluster. It decouples the compute, storage, and metadata layers: Compute Layer Each Tabsdata Function runs as an isolated process on the Tabsdata server's Kubernetes cluster. Built atop Polars Lazyframe Architecture, Lazy evaluation and streaming capabilities allow each worker handle large datasets without being constrained by memory limits. Storage Layer Tabular data can be stored on local file storage, in a cloud provider, or spread across several providers such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, or a network file system. Scale storage independently from Compute Metadata Layer Projects, Collections, Functions, Tables, Execution Logs, Error History, Code Versioning, and more can be stored locally, in the cloud, or distributed across multiple systems

Tabsdata reaches external systems through connectors, allowing the decoupling of inter-system and intra-system operations. Tabsdata comes with many Connectors out-of-the-box, or you can build your own with plugins.

Authorization uses a direct permission model: permissions are granted straight to a user, with no roles in between. See Permissions for the levels and CLI commands. All credentials live in a credentials store: both Tabsdata's own credentials and the credentials for your connections to external systems. note Even when you provide a credential inline, Tabsdata extracts it into the credentials store. Credentials are never stored in the clear.

Tabsdata runs on Linux for production, and macOS or Windows for development. A server's Kubernetes cluster comes from one of four providers, set with --provider: kminus: a lightweight, modified Kubernetes that runs pods as native processes in a Python environment instead of Docker. The default for local development; needs no root or admin access. docker: the Kubernetes cluster bundled with Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows). eks: AWS EKS. Because the same binary runs against any of them, what you build locally against kminus behaves the same once deployed to a real cluster.

Tabsdata was designed from the ground up to integrate with AI, through a Tabsdata MCP server that exposes Tabsdata to AI agents, backed by a skills library and a vector database. See Connect an AI Agent to set it up. There are two ways to use it: A built-in agent handles operational tasks inside Tabsdata. Your own coding agents (Claude, Gemini, Codex) connect through the MCP server. The authorization model is fully integrated with the MCP server. When an agent acts on your behalf, it can do exactly what you are authorized to do, and nothing more. Collections store Functions, Tables, and Connections. Collection Purpose, Behaviour and Architecture varies depending on whether they store Publisher, Transformers, or Subscribers

Transformer collections store Transformer functions, which read input data from Tabsdata Tables and write output data into other Tabsdata Tables. Transformer Collections can store one or more Tabsdata Functions. Since no calls to external systems are made through these collections, they do not require a Connection to be bound to it. The main purpose of Transformer collections is that they define commit behavior during Execution Plans. For more information, view [Pristine State] and [Transactions] collection · world? collection · insights · data product? ▶ Trigger transformer Table country ? //world Committed Table city ? //world Committed Transformer find_big_cities ? Table big_cities ? //insights No versions yet

Publisher Collections store Publisher Functions, which read input data from external systems and write output data into Tabsdata Tables. While Publishers connect to external systems, they do not contain any credentials to those systems, which are stored in a separate object called a connection The main purpose of Publisher Collections is to bind a Publisher to a Connection, allowing the Function to use the credentials stored in that Connection Unlike Transformer Collections, Publisher Collections can only hold one Publisher at a time and must also have a Connection bound to it. Tabsdata server collection · world? ▶ Trigger publisher Database PostgreSQL ? PostgreSQL · external Reachable Connection conn-postgres.yaml ? Publisher read_world ? Table country ? //world No versions yet Table city ? //world No versions yet

Subscriber Collections store Subscriber Functions, which read input data from Tabsdata Tables and write output data to external systems. While Subscribers connect to external systems, they do not contain any credentials for those systems. Instead, credentials are stored in a separate object called a Connection. The main purpose of Subscriber Collections is to bind a Subscriber to a Connection, allowing the Function to use the credentials stored in that Connection. Unlike Transformer Collections, Subscriber Collections can only hold one Subscriber at a time and must also have a Connection bound to them. Tabsdata's agentic workflow uses an MCP server so a coding agent builds and runs your workflows for you. Install it into your agent before continuing to QuickStart. Claude Code and Codex are currently supported. Step 1Install the MCP server Start the agent from a shell whose virtual environment has Tabsdata installed. Temporary, for 2.0.0 The MCP server needs tabsdata-agent, which ships as its own package and is not yet pulled in by tabsdata[all]. For 2.0.0 it also has to be installed from the Tabsdata package index with the version pinned. Set the index first. This is needed whichever installer you use: export PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL=https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ export UV_INDEX=https://pypi.tabsdata.com/simple/ export UV_INDEX_STRATEGY=unsafe-best-match Then install the Tabsdata agent if you have not done so yet: uv pip uv pip install tabsdata-agent==2.0.0 pip install tabsdata-agent==2.0.0 Install Tabsdata covers this as part of the full install, so skip this if you followed that page. These additional steps will not be required once Tabsdata 2.0.0 is on PyPI Claude Code Codex claude mcp add tabsdata -- python -m tabsdatak.ag.mcp - Linux / macOS Windows PowerShell Windows cmd.exe codex mcp add tabsdata -- "$(python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)')" -m tabsdatak.ag.mcp - codex mcp add tabsdata -- (python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)") -m tabsdatak.ag.mcp - for /f "delims=" %i in ('python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"') do codex mcp add tabsdata -- "%i" -m tabsdatak.ag.mcp - Step 2Using the agent You need an active session with the Tabsdata server before starting your agent. Log in, then start it from the same terminal: Claude Code Codex tdk login --server localhost --user admin --password tabsdata claude tdk login --server localhost --user admin --password tabsdata codex The agent authenticates through your session, so it can only do what you're authorized to do.
